etymology: Hebrew machanayim, “two camps” or “two hosts,” the name Jacob gave to the place where the host of God met him as he returned to the land.
biblical_def: Mahanaim was a town east of the Jordan, on the border between Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, that took its name from the day Jacob, returning from Padan-aram in fear of Esau, was met by the angels of God. When he saw them he said, “This is God’s host,” and called the place Mahanaim, “two camps” (Gen 32:2), as though the LORD had set His own encampment beside the patriarch’s. Long after, when Joshua portioned the land, Mahanaim was numbered among the cities given to the Levites out of the tribe of Gad (Jos 21:38). It became a place of refuge in Israel’s troubled days: thither Abner brought Ish-bosheth to reign, and thither David fled from Absalom and was sustained by Barzillai and the men of Gilead until the rebellion was broken (2Sa 17:24). The dictionary records Mahanaim not for its stones but for its testimony, that the same God who pitched His camp beside a fearful Jacob is the God who hides His servants in the day of trouble. The lines were fallen unto this little town in a pleasant place, and it stands as a witness that the bounds of the saint’s habitation are set by Him who keeps watch over His own.

etymology: Hebrew peniel, “the face of God,” the name Jacob gave to the place where he wrestled until the breaking of the day and saw God face to face.
biblical_def: Penuel, also written Peniel, was a place east of the Jordan, near the brook Jabbok, where Jacob, left alone in the night before he met Esau, wrestled with a man until the breaking of the day. When the stranger touched the hollow of his thigh and yet Jacob would not let Him go without a blessing, he called the name of the place Penuel, saying, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved” (Gen 32:30). He passed over Penuel halting upon his thigh as the sun rose upon him, a prince who had power with God and had prevailed, marked for ever by the encounter. In later days a tower stood at Penuel, and Gideon, returning from the slaughter of the Midianites, broke it down when its men refused him bread (Jdg 8:17). Long after, Jeroboam built Penuel as he fortified his rebel kingdom (1Ki 12:25). The dictionary honours Penuel chiefly for that night by the Jabbok, when the LORD met a man, broke him, and blessed him in the same hour. It stands as a witness that the bounds of the saint’s habitation are appointed by Him before whose face we live, and that the place of our deepest wrestling may become the place where we behold His mercy.

etymology: Hebrew tsarethan, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “their distress” or “cooling,” a town in the valley of the Jordan near where the waters parted for Israel.
biblical_def: Zarethan was a town in the plain of the Jordan, named in the great account of Israel’s crossing into the land of promise. When the feet of the priests bearing the ark touched the brim of the swollen river, the waters that came down from above stood and rose up in a heap, very far from the city Adam that is beside Zarethan, while the waters that ran down toward the sea of the plain failed and were cut off (Jos 3:16). So the people passed over on dry ground, and Zarethan stood near the very spot where the LORD made a path through the flood. In the days of Solomon the brass for the vessels of the temple was cast in the clay ground of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan (1Ki 7:46), so that the town is bound up both with the conquest and with the building of the house of God. The dictionary records Zarethan that the reader may see how the LORD threaded His purposes through small and forgotten places. The lines were fallen unto this valley town in a pleasant place, and it bears witness that the same God who heaped up the Jordan for His people sets the bounds of every habitation, and that no portion of the land was too obscure to serve His unfolding work.

etymology: Hebrew tsaanannim, perhaps “wanderings” or “removings,” marking the plain or oak of Zaanaim near Kedesh in the land of Naphtali.
biblical_def: Zaanannim was a place on the border of the tribe of Naphtali, marked by a plain, or as some read it an oak, near the city of Kedesh. When Joshua divided the land by lot, the coast of Naphtali was described as running from Heleph and from Allon to Zaanannim and onward to the borders of the tribe (Jos 19:33), so that the town stood as a known landmark in the apportioning of the inheritance. It comes again into the sacred history in the days of Deborah and Barak, for Heber the Kenite, who had severed himself from the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, pitched his tent near the plain of Zaanaim, and it was in his tent that Sisera, fleeing from the host of the LORD, met his end at the hand of Jael (Jdg 4:11). The dictionary records Zaanannim that the reader may see how the LORD set His landmarks in the land and ordered even the tent of a wandering Kenite to His purpose. The lines were fallen unto Naphtali in pleasant places, and this border town bears witness that the bounds of the people were set by Him who divided to the nations their inheritance and overrules the smallest place to the glory of His name.

etymology: Hebrew seneh, “thorn” or “bramble,” the name of a sharp rock or crag in the pass by Michmash.
biblical_def: Seneh was the name of one of two sharp rocks, or crags, that stood in the narrow pass between Michmash and Gibeah, where Jonathan with his armourbearer climbed up against the garrison of the Philistines. The two crags are named in the sacred record, “the forefront of the one was situate northward over against Michmash, and the other southward over against Gibeah,” and the south crag was called Seneh (1Sa 14:4-5). It was a place of fear and difficulty, a craggy passage where a man must climb upon his hands and feet, yet Jonathan went up trusting that the LORD could save by many or by few, and the LORD wrought a great deliverance that day. The dictionary records Seneh, the thorny rock, that the reader may see how the LORD chooses the hard and forbidding place to display His salvation. The lines fell to Benjamin in pleasant places, yet some of those places were sharp crags, and the name Seneh, the bramble, reminds us that the path of faith often runs over rough ground. It bears witness that no rock is too steep for the people of a sovereign God, who determines the bounds of the battle and gives the victory where He pleases.

etymology: Hebrew mearah, “a cave,” a place beside the Sidonians named among the land yet to be possessed.
biblical_def: Mearah was a place beside the Sidonians, named in the account of the land that yet remained to be possessed when Joshua was old and stricken in years. The LORD told him that very much land remained, and among the borders He named was the coast of the Sidonians and “Mearah that is beside the Sidonians, unto Aphek, to the borders of the Amorites” (Jos 13:4). So Mearah stood at the northern edge of the inheritance, in the region toward Sidon and Lebanon, a portion promised to Israel though not yet taken. Its name signifies a cave, and it may have been a place of caves along that mountainous coast. The dictionary records Mearah that the reader may see how the LORD held out to His people more than they had yet laid hold of, and how the bounds of the promise reached even to the borders of the heathen cities. The lines were fallen unto Israel in pleasant places, but much of the goodly heritage remained to be entered by faith. Mearah bears witness that the inheritance of the saints is sure in the promise of God even where it is not yet possessed, and that He who determines the bounds of habitation will give His people all that He has appointed them to receive.

etymology: Hebrew punon, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “darkness” or “perplexity,” a wilderness station of Israel in their journeys.
biblical_def: Punon was one of the encampments of Israel in the wilderness, named in the record of their journeys that Moses wrote by the commandment of the LORD. As the people came up from the bondage of Egypt toward the borders of Edom, they pitched at Zalmonah, and then removed and pitched in Punon, and from Punon they journeyed and pitched in Oboth (Num 33:42-43). It lay in the desert region toward the land of Edom, one stage in the long wandering through which the LORD led and humbled and proved His people, to know what was in their heart. The dictionary records Punon, a bare name in a list of camps, that the reader may see how every stage of the pilgrimage was numbered and appointed by God. Not one resting place was forgotten, not one removal unordered; the cloud went before, and where it stayed, there Israel pitched. The lines of the wilderness journey were measured by the hand that determines the bounds of habitation, and Punon bears witness that the LORD knows the way that His people take, leading them by a right way to the city of their inheritance. The pilgrim saint may read this forgotten camp and be assured that his own stages, however bare, are numbered by his God.

etymology: Hebrew chadid, “sharp” or “pointed,” a town of Benjamin reinhabited by the children of the captivity after the return from Babylon.
biblical_def: Hadid was a town in the territory of Benjamin, lying toward the western lowland, that is named among the places reinhabited by the children of the captivity when they came up out of Babylon. In the great register of those who returned with Zerubbabel, the men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono are numbered together (Ezr 2:33), and the same households appear again in the parallel record of Nehemiah (Neh 7:37), and once more among the villages where the men of Benjamin dwelt after the wall was built (Neh 11:34). So Hadid is a town of the restoration, a place repeopled by the mercy of God after the long desolation of the exile. The dictionary records Hadid that the reader may behold the faithfulness of the LORD, who did not cast off His people for ever, but brought a remnant home to the old inheritance and set them again in their cities. The lines that had fallen to Benjamin in pleasant places were possessed afresh, the ancient landmarks were owned again, and Hadid was numbered once more among the dwellings of the covenant people. It bears witness that the God who scatters in judgment gathers in mercy, and keeps the bounds of His people’s habitation even through captivity and return.

etymology: Hebrew yehud, perhaps “praised” or “Judah-like,” a town in the allotment of the tribe of Dan.
biblical_def: Jehud was a town given to the tribe of Dan when Joshua divided the land by lot. The coast of the children of Dan is described as taking in Jehud, Bene-berak, and Gath-rimmon among the cities of their inheritance (Jos 19:45), in the lowland country toward the great sea. Dan received a small portion among the tribes, and the children of Dan afterward found their coast too little for them, yet the lot of the LORD had fallen, and Jehud was numbered among the towns first appointed to them. The dictionary records Jehud, a bare name in the apportioning of Dan, that the reader may see how the LORD measured out the land tribe by tribe and town by town. Not the casting of the lot, nor the strength of the tribe, but the appointing of God set the bounds of every portion; the lot was cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof was of the LORD. The lines were fallen unto Dan in pleasant places, and this little town bears witness that the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance numbered even Jehud among the goodly heritage, and that no portion of His people’s land was beneath the care of Him who apportioned it.

etymology: Hebrew nobach, perhaps “a barking” or “prominent,” the name a Manassite gave both to himself and to the eastern town he took.
biblical_def: Nobah was both a man of the tribe of Manasseh and the town that he took and named after himself in the land east of the Jordan. As Israel possessed the kingdom of Bashan and the country of Gilead, the children of Machir and of Manasseh seized the villages of the region, and Nobah went and took Kenath and the villages thereof, and called it Nobah, after his own name (Num 32:42). The town stood in the eastern reaches of Manasseh’s portion, on the desert frontier, and it comes again into the sacred history in the days of Gideon, for he went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and smote the host of Midian which lay secure (Jdg 8:11). The dictionary records Nobah that the reader may see how the LORD gave His people room in the wide eastern country and set their bounds even on the edge of the wilderness. The lines were fallen unto Manasseh in pleasant places, and this frontier town bears witness that the same God who determines the bounds of habitation gave even the far borders of the inheritance into the hand of His people, and that no portion of the land lay beyond His apportioning care.

It witnesses to the LORD’s gift of room to His people even on the borders of the desert.
